name: AI in Health Economics and Outcomes Research
blurb: Using AI to show a medicine's value to payers.
title: AI in Health Economics and Outcomes Research
answer: Health economics teams use machine learning to predict outcomes and costs from health record time series and to find subgroups where a treatment delivers different value, sometimes called precision HEOR. Payers and health technology assessment bodies still expect transparent methods they can reproduce.

reading.body:
Health economics teams use machine learning to predict outcomes and costs from health record time series and to find subgroups where a treatment delivers different value, but payers still expect methods they can reproduce.

The pattern is a split between what the models can do and what the buyer will accept. Machine learning supports outcome prediction and patient stratification, the two uses a 2020 review in PMC identified. The same techniques that make those predictions possible also make them harder to explain, and the party deciding whether to pay for a medicine is not the party that built the model.

For AI specifically, this is a case where capability is not the constraint. The constraint is legibility to a health technology assessment body. A model that finds a subgroup benefiting more from a treatment is only useful if the method behind it survives review, which is why interpretable models are favoured for value dossiers. A payer who cannot follow the method will discount the result.

The data covers one review from 2020 and the general shape of the field. It does not name the models, the diseases, the payers, or any outcome achieved, and it gives no evidence on whether interpretable methods have actually won in practice.

terms.line: The subset of AI focused on systems that learn from data and improve with experience rather than following explicitly programmed rules. Nearly everything called AI in production is machine learning underneath.

sections.heading: What it means for a commercial team

explainer:
Health economics and outcomes research shows payers and health technology assessment bodies what a treatment achieves and at what cost: clinical outcomes, quality of life, resource use and value for money. Its outputs, such as cost effectiveness models and value dossiers, influence whether and at what price a medicine is reimbursed.

Machine learning helps predict outcomes and costs from real world data, identify patient subgroups where value differs, and speed literature reviews and model building. Payers and assessment bodies, though, need to understand and reproduce the analysis, so interpretable methods and transparent reporting matter more here than raw predictive power.

developments.text: A review in PMC set out machine learning uses in HEOR, including outcome prediction and patient stratification for precision HEOR.
